intro_en:
This is one of the most beautiful segments of the Israel National Trail, with unique desert scenery. Canyons, cliffs and mountains of granite, sandstone and limestone create an especially colourful geological celebration, ending with a view over the Gulf of Eilat.

 Be'er Ora - Shehoret (54)
 Har Yehoram - Eilat (56)
character_en: (For those walking from north to south) Gentle climbs through canyons, with a few challenging sections that are not difficult. In addition, 2 short and slightly steep climbs.
pois_en: Shehoret Canyon, Har Shehoret viewpoint, the "Lost Valley", Ein Netafim
important_en: At the campsite at the start of Shehoret Canyon there should be a water trailer (a tank for filling up with water) in the evening hours. It is worth confirming this with the regional ranger of the Israel Nature and Parks Authority (INPA). The road to the campsite is passable for an ordinary car.
At the Har Yehoram campsite there should be a water trailer placed by the Israel Nature and Parks Authority (INPA). Before setting out, it is worth confirming this with the regional INPA ranger.
description_en:
From the overnight campsite in Nahal Shehoret we head west to the mouth of Shehoret Canyon, a few minutes' walk away. The Israel National Trail continues into the granite canyon, which offers a close encounter with basement rocks - rocks formed from the molten magmatic material beneath the Earth's crust. These are the oldest rocks exposed in the Eilat Mountains, and they stand out in their dark colours: black, grey and shades of red.
We advance through the canyon up Nahal Shehoret for about 1.5 km. On the way we hop without difficulty over several low waterfalls.
On leaving the canyon, the colour of the rocks changes sharply. The light-coloured rocks are sedimentary rocks, and the transition line between them and the dark rocks is a fault line. The block of basement rock through which Nahal Shehoret carved Shehoret Canyon was uplifted relative to the western side of the fault line, which is why the young sedimentary rocks appear on the surface alongside the ancient basement rocks.
The Israel National Trail turns south along a red-marked trail and climbs along the fault line. The trail passes between the two sides of the fault: on the right we see sedimentary rocks and on the left basement rocks - a few steps spanning millions of years in the geological chronology.
The climb to the saddle at the foot of Har Shehoret is relatively easy. From the top of the saddle there is a fine view: north to Har Amir, east to the Arava, and to the south the continuation of the fault line is visible all the way to the horizon - in the saddle between the dark Har Shlomo and the light-coloured Har Yehoram.
We descend from the saddle to Nahal Roded, which runs parallel to Nahal Shehoret to the south. In the wide channel there is a trail junction. A black-marked trail heading north-west leads to a beautiful and special canyon that is well worth a detour from the trail. The canyon, known as the "Lost Valley" and by another popular name, "Canyon of the Stripes", is a short channel cut into sandstone, with stripes and rocks of varied colours visible in its walls.
The Israel National Trail continues south on a blue-marked trail, climbing gently alongside a tributary of Nahal Roded. At the junction with a black-marked trail, the blue trail turns west towards the border road, Road 12. A short distance from the junction, the blue trail passes an archaeological site called Horvat Bodeda, with the remains of a large quarry from the Byzantine period. The Israel National Trail continues south with black markings to Nahal Netafim.
After a short walk we begin the descent to Nahal Netafim along one of its northern tributaries. When we reach the main channel of Nahal Netafim, we turn west up the stream with green markings.
The Israel National Trail winds with the meanders of the stream. After meeting a black-marked trail, we climb with the green markings up to the northern bank, for a bypass.
Above the streambed, for those who enjoy a challenge, the black trail continues along the streambed, passing between large boulders and several waterfalls, in less comfortable walking for about 1.5 km, which takes considerably longer - until another meeting between the black trail and the Israel National Trail with the green markings.
A short distance before Ein Netafim, the Israel National Trail turns south along a red-marked trail that climbs out of the streambed. It is highly recommended to continue with the green markings a short distance inside the channel, to a high waterfall at the foot of which Ein Netafim emerges.
In Arabic the spring is called Ein al-Qatar, meaning the Spring of Drops. The spring's water drips into a concrete pool adorned with maidenhair fern. Despite its low discharge, the spring is the only water source in a large desert expanse, and ibex, hyraxes and desert birds come to drink from its water. It is therefore especially important that we keep the spring and its surroundings clean and refrain from bathing in it. The spring water is not fit for drinking.
After climbing out of the channel on the red trail, the Israel National Trail continues with black markings parallel to a northern tributary of Nahal Netafim. At the end of the climb we reach a saddle beneath a conical dome.
Here the Israel National Trail leaves the black trail and turns west towards Road 12. However, to reach the end point at the overnight campsite at Har Yehoram, continue from the saddle on a short walk downhill with the black markings.
nearby_en: Har Yoash rises about 70 m above Road 12 and the Israel National Trail. A wonderful viewpoint that can be reached by climbing up a jeep track.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
